claim: Reduced expression of TP53 and RB1 allowed induced PNECs to form subcutaneous growths in immune-deficient mice.
source: Although reduced expression of the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1 allowed the induced PNECs to form subcutaneous growths in immune-deficient mice, the tumors did not display the aggressive characteristics of SCLC seen in human patients.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from previous work, supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Tumors from TP53/RB1-deficient PNECs did not display the aggressive characteristics of SCLC seen in human patients.
source: Although reduced expression of the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1 allowed the induced PNECs to form subcutaneous growths in immune-deficient mice, the tumors did not display the aggressive characteristics of SCLC seen in human patients.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract comparing tumor behavior to human SCLC characteristics.

claim: Doxycycline-regulated expression of wild-type or mutant MYC protein promotes rapid growth, invasion, and metastasis of hESC-derived cells after injection into the renal capsule.
source: Here, we report that the additional, doxycycline-regulated expression of a transgene encoding wild-type or mutant MYC protein promotes rapid growth, invasion, and metastasis of these hESC-derived cells after injection into the renal capsule.
evidence: Primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of MYC encourages the formation of the SCLC-N subtype, marked by high levels of NEUROD1 RNA.
source: Similar to others, we find that the addition of MYC encourages the formation of the SCLC-N subtype, marked by high levels of NEUROD1 RNA.
evidence: Stated finding in the abstract, supported by transcriptional profiling data and comparison to published literature.

claim: The subtype of SCLC does not change upon metastatic spread.
source: Using paired primary and metastatic samples for RNA-sequencing, we observe that the subtype of SCLC does not change upon metastatic spread and that production of NEUROD1 is maintained.
evidence: Finding from RNA-sequencing analysis of paired samples presented in the study.

claim: Production of NEUROD1 is maintained upon metastatic spread.
source: Using paired primary and metastatic samples for RNA-sequencing, we observe that the subtype of SCLC does not change upon metastatic spread and that production of NEUROD1 is maintained.
evidence: Finding from RNA-sequencing analysis of paired samples presented in the study.

claim: Transformation of chicken embryo fibroblasts by Rous sarcoma virus exemplifies models that lack verisimilitude but nevertheless have revealed major features of carcinogenesis.
source: The transformation of chicken embryo fibroblasts by Rous sarcoma virus or the induction of leukemias with various murine leukemia viruses exemplifies models that lack verisimilitude but nevertheless have revealed major features of carcinogenesis (Varmus and Weinberg, 1993).
evidence: Historical example cited from published literature to support discussion of model systems.

claim: Induction of leukemias with various murine leukemia viruses exemplifies models that lack verisimilitude but nevertheless have revealed major features of carcinogenesis.
source: The transformation of chicken embryo fibroblasts by Rous sarcoma virus or the induction of leukemias with various murine leukemia viruses exemplifies models that lack verisimilitude but nevertheless have revealed major features of carcinogenesis (Varmus and Weinberg, 1993).
evidence: Historical example cited from published literature to support discussion of model systems.

claim: Techniques for generating, propagating, and differentiating human stem cells have raised the possibility of studying carcinogenesis in a wide variety of human cell lineages.
source: Techniques for generating, propagating, and differentiating human stem cells – either tissue-specific stem cells or pluripotent stem cells – have raised the possibility of studying carcinogenesis in a wide variety of human cell lineages, as initially demonstrated for gliomas derived from induced human pluripotent stem cells (Funato et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about technological advances supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gliomas can be derived from induced human pluripotent stem cells.
source: Techniques for generating, propagating, and differentiating human stem cells – either tissue-specific stem cells or pluripotent stem cells – have raised the possibility of studying carcinogenesis in a wide variety of human cell lineages, as initially demonstrated for gliomas derived from induced human pluripotent stem cells (Funato et al., 2014).
evidence: Example cited from published literature demonstrating stem cell-derived cancer models.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells can be efficiently differentiated into mature lung epithelial cells.
source: We have recently attempted to study the mechanisms by which small cell lung cancer (SCLC) arises in human lung cells by efficiently differentiating human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2014) into mature lung epithelial cells, including the likely precursor of SCLC (pulmonary neuroendocrine cells [PNECs]) and then simulating loss of function of the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1, tumor suppressors commonly lost in human SCLC (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of prior work by the authors, supported by citations to their previous publications.

claim: Pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (PNECs) are the likely precursor of SCLC.
source: We have recently attempted to study the mechanisms by which small cell lung cancer (SCLC) arises in human lung cells by efficiently differentiating human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2014) into mature lung epithelial cells, including the likely precursor of SCLC (pulmonary neuroendocrine cells [PNECs]) and then simulating loss of function of the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1, tumor suppressors commonly lost in human SCLC (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement based on established understanding in the field, supported by the authors' prior work.

claim: TP53 and RB1 are tumor suppressors commonly lost in human SCLC.
source: We have recently attempted to study the mechanisms by which small cell lung cancer (SCLC) arises in human lung cells by efficiently differentiating human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) (Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2014) into mature lung epithelial cells, including the likely precursor of SCLC (pulmonary neuroendocrine cells [PNECs]) and then simulating loss of function of the tumor suppressor genes TP53 and RB1, tumor suppressors commonly lost in human SCLC (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge about SCLC genetics, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PNEC-like cells that have lost the function of TP53 and RB1 can form tumors subcutaneously in immunodeficient mice.
source: PNEC-like cells that have lost the function of these two tumor suppressor genes, by expression of short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) specific for RB1 and TP53, can form tumors subcutaneously in immunodeficient mice; however, these tumors grow slowly and do not invade or metastasize, standing in contrast to what is known about the clinical presentation and behavior of SCLC (Budczies et al., 2015).
evidence: Finding from the authors' prior work, supported by data and citation.

claim: Tumors from TP53/RB1-deficient PNEC-like cells grow slowly and do not invade or metastasize.
source: PNEC-like cells that have lost the function of these two tumor suppressor genes, by expression of short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) specific for RB1 and TP53, can form tumors subcutaneously in immunodeficient mice; however, these tumors grow slowly and do not invade or metastasize, standing in contrast to what is known about the clinical presentation and behavior of SCLC (Budczies et al., 2015).
evidence: Observational finding from the authors' experiments, contrasted with known SCLC behavior.

claim: The original hESC-derived SCLC models appeared to be benign growths that do not resemble SCLCs functionally.
source: Thus, the original hESC-derived SCLC models we generated appeared to be benign growths that do not resemble SCLCs functionally, limiting their utility as models for aggressive human SCLC.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Full transformation of PNECs to form malignant SCLC requires additional changes beyond restricted expression of RB1 and TP53.
source: Our earlier findings are consistent with the idea that full transformation of PNECs to form malignant SCLC requires additional changes beyond restricted expression of the tumor suppressor genes RB1 and TP53, such as heightened expression of a proto-oncogene in the MYC family (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from the authors' findings, supported by citations to related work.

claim: Heightened expression of a proto-oncogene in the MYC family is an additional change that may be required for full transformation of PNECs to form malignant SCLC.
source: Our earlier findings are consistent with the idea that full transformation of PNECs to form malignant SCLC requires additional changes beyond restricted expression of the tumor suppressor genes RB1 and TP53, such as heightened expression of a proto-oncogene in the MYC family (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to prior work and the authors' experimental design.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells injected into renal capsules of immunodeficient mice produced rapidly expanding tumors that invaded locally.
source: When these cells were then injected into renal capsules of immunodeficient mice, some produced rapidly expanding tumors that invaded locally and sometimes formed metastatic growths, mostly in the liver.
evidence: Primary experimental finding reported in the introduction.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells injected into renal capsules sometimes formed metastatic growths, mostly in the liver.
source: When these cells were then injected into renal capsules of immunodeficient mice, some produced rapidly expanding tumors that invaded locally and sometimes formed metastatic growths, mostly in the liver.
evidence: Primary experimental finding reported in the introduction.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells contain dramatically reduced amounts of TP53 and RB1 proteins as a result of DOX induction of shRNAs specific for these tumor suppressor mRNAs.
source: As expected, both cell lines also contained dramatically reduced amounts of TP53 and RB1 proteins as a result of DOX induction of shRNAs specific for these tumor suppressor mRNAs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental result confirmed by western blot shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells can produce MYC protein after addition of DOX.
source: The ability of the RPM and RPM (T58A) cells to produce MYC protein was documented by western blotting of cell extracts prepared 72 hr after addition of DOX (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental result confirmed by western blot shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PNECs from cultures of RP lines of RUES2 cells produced small benign lesions subcutaneously without invasion or metastasis.
source: As previously reported, PNECs from cultures of RP lines of RUES2 cells produced small benign lesions subcutaneously without invasion or metastasis.
evidence: Reference to previously reported findings, confirmed in current experiments.

claim: Similar findings were observed when RP cells were injected into the renal capsule.
source: Similar findings were observed when these cells were injected into the renal capsule (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental observation reported with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The volumes of RPM and RPM (T58A)-derived tumors quickly exceeded the volumes of RP-derived tumors.
source: We noted that the volumes of RPM and RPM (T58A)-derived tumors quickly exceeded the volumes of RP-derived tumors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental observation from tumor growth monitoring, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rapid growth of RPM tumors was dependent on continuous provision of DOX in the diet.
source: The rapid growth of RPM tumors was dependent on continuous provision of DOX in the diet.
evidence: Experimental finding from DOX withdrawal and add-back experiments.

claim: Animals on a DOX-free diet engrafted subcutaneously with RPM or RPM (T58A) cells failed to produce tumors.
source: If animals on a DOX-free diet were engrafted subcutaneously with RPM or RPM (T58A) cells, they failed to produce tumors (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Experimental result from DOX withdrawal experiment, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in some mice engrafted with RPM or RPM (T58A) cells if the animals were placed on a DOX-containing diet up to 2 months after injection.
source: However, tumor growth was observed in some mice engrafted with such cells if the animals were placed on a DOX-containing diet up to 2 months after injection (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: Experimental result from DOX add-back experiment, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At least some of the RPM cells remained viable and responsive to the oncogenic effects of depleting RB1 and TP53 and producing MYC.
source: These findings suggest that at least some of the RPM cells remained viable and responsive to the oncogenic effects of depleting RB1 and TP53 and producing MYC.
evidence: Inference drawn from the DOX add-back experiment results.

claim: The rapid growth and morphological features of RPM and RPM (T58A) tumors were histologically consistent with SCLC.
source: The rapid growth and morphological features of RPM and RPM (T58A) tumors in these experiments were histologically consistent with SCLC.
evidence: Histological analysis of tumor samples.

claim: Subcutaneous injection did not produce metastatic disease to the liver.
source: Critically, subcutaneous injection did not produce metastatic disease to the liver (not shown), nor was there evidence of gross metastases to the lungs in any of the mice examined (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental observation from histological examination.

claim: There was no evidence of gross metastases to the lungs in any of the mice examined after subcutaneous injection.
source: Critically, subcutaneous injection did not produce metastatic disease to the liver (not shown), nor was there evidence of gross metastases to the lungs in any of the mice examined (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental observation from histological examination, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SCLC-like tumors composed of RUES2-derived RPM cells may require a different microenvironment for metastatic seeding.
source: These findings suggest that SCLC-like tumors composed of RUES2-derived RPM cells grow rapidly after subcutaneous implantation, but may require a different microenvironment, such as the vascular-rich, highly perfused renal capsule (Bogden et al., 1979; Sobczuk et al., 2020), providing a more hospitable environment for metastatic seeding.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations, supported by citations about renal capsule characteristics.

claim: The renal capsule is vascular-rich and highly perfused.
source: These findings suggest that SCLC-like tumors composed of RUES2-derived RPM cells grow rapidly after subcutaneous implantation, but may require a different microenvironment, such as the vascular-rich, highly perfused renal capsule (Bogden et al., 1979; Sobczuk et al., 2020), providing a more hospitable environment for metastatic seeding.
evidence: Established knowledge about renal capsule anatomy, supported by citations.

claim: RPM tumors were notable for increased vascularization, larger volume, and invasion into surrounding endothelium compared to RP tumors.
source: RPM tumors, as compared to RP tumors, were notable for increased vascularization, larger volume, and invasion into surrounding endothelium.
evidence: Comparative histological and morphological observations.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) PNECs injected into the renal capsule of immunocompromised mice displayed frequent metastasis to the liver.
source: RPM and RPM (T58A) PNECs injected into the renal capsule of immunocompromised mice also displayed frequent metastasis to the liver (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental observation from renal capsule injection experiments, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Approximately half of animals administered DOX developed metastases in distant organs, including the liver or lung.
source: In animals administered DOX, histological examinations showed that approximately half developed metastases in distant organs, including the liver or lung.
evidence: Quantitative finding from histological examination of experimental animals.

claim: One of the mice developed metastatic tumors in both liver and lung sites.
source: One of the mice developed metastatic tumors in both liver and lung sites (Figure 1D).
evidence: Specific observation from experimental animals, referenced in Figure 1D.

claim: No metastases were observed in the bone, brain, or lymph nodes.
source: No metastases were observed in the bone, brain, or lymph nodes.
evidence: Negative finding from histological examination of experimental animals.

claim: Metastatic lesions had similar proliferative character and expression of MYC compared to their paired primary counterparts.
source: Metastatic lesions were characterized as having similar proliferative character and expression of MYC, as well as comparable expression of the neuronal markers NCAM (CD56) and NEUROD1 compared to their paired primary counterparts (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis of paired primary and metastatic samples, shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: Metastatic lesions had comparable expression of the neuronal markers NCAM (CD56) and NEUROD1 compared to their paired primary counterparts.
source: Metastatic lesions were characterized as having similar proliferative character and expression of MYC, as well as comparable expression of the neuronal markers NCAM (CD56) and NEUROD1 compared to their paired primary counterparts (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis of paired primary and metastatic samples, shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: ASCL1 expression was absent in RPM and RPM (T58A) tumors at both primary and metastatic sites.
source: In contrast, ASCL1 expression was absent in RPM and RPM (T58A) tumors at both primary and metastatic sites (Figure 3F).
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The majority of cells in RP tumors showed positive ASCL1 expression but lacked NEUROD1 expression.
source: Meanwhile, the majority of cells in RP tumors showed positive ASCL1 expression but lacked NEUROD1 expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: MYC expression may facilitate the transition of SCLC tumors from the classical ASCL1-driven subtype to the NEUROD1 variant.
source: These findings suggest that MYC expression may facilitate the transition of SCLC tumors from the classical ASCL1-driven subtype to the NEUROD1 variant.
evidence: Inference drawn from the differential expression patterns of ASCL1 and NEUROD1 in RP versus RPM tumors.

claim: Both the site of implantation of cells and the addition of a driver oncogene were required to produce vigorous growth and metastatic spread of SCLC-like tumors.
source: Thus, both the site of implantation of cells and the addition of a driver oncogene were required to produce vigorous growth and metastatic spread of SCLC-like tumors, and the metastatic lesions retained histological and immunohistochemical features of the primary tumors.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the experimental comparisons of injection sites and genotypes.

claim: The metastatic lesions retained histological and immunohistochemical features of the primary tumors.
source: Thus, both the site of implantation of cells and the addition of a driver oncogene were required to produce vigorous growth and metastatic spread of SCLC-like tumors, and the metastatic lesions retained histological and immunohistochemical features of the primary tumors.
evidence: Conclusion from comparative histological and immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: Three dominant cell-type groups were observed in transcriptional space: a basal-like cluster marked by expression of KRT19, a fibroblast-like cluster marked by expression of COL1A1, and a neuroendocrine differentiation cluster marked by expression of ASCL1.
source: By integrating previously published RUES2-derived RP single-cell data (Chen et al., 2019), we observed three dominant cell-type groups in transcriptional space, using reference mapping, enrichment analysis, and manual curation to identify cell lineage likelihood: a basal-like cluster marked by expression of KRT19, a fibroblast-like cluster marked by expression of COL1A1, and the most prominent cluster of cells appearing to have features of neuroendocrine differentiation, marked by expression of the neuroendocrine lineage defining transcription factor ASCL1 (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cells within the neuroendocrine differentiation cluster expressed ASCL1 and NEUROD1.
source: Comparing the recently described SCLC subtype markers (Rudin et al., 2019) across these datasets showed that cells within the neuroendocrine differentiation cluster cells expressed ASCL1 and NEUROD1, whereas POU2F3 RNA was not detected.
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis comparing SCLC subtype markers.

claim: POU2F3 RNA was not detected in cells within the neuroendocrine differentiation cluster.
source: Comparing the recently described SCLC subtype markers (Rudin et al., 2019) across these datasets showed that cells within the neuroendocrine differentiation cluster cells expressed ASCL1 and NEUROD1, whereas POU2F3 RNA was not detected.
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis comparing SCLC subtype markers.

claim: Levels of YAP1 RNA were variable and were not co-expressed with either ASCL1 or NEUROD1.
source: Levels of YAP1 RNA were variable and were not co-expressed with either ASCL1 or NEUROD1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: YAP1 expression was mostly attributed to fibroblast- and basal-like cells that are often observed in long-term cultures of differentiated hESCs.
source: YAP1 expression was mostly attributed to fibroblast- and basal-like cells that are often observed in long-term cultures of differentiated hESCs (Figure 4B; Huang et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Dye et al., 2015; Rodrigues Toste de Carvalho et al., 2021).
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis, supported by citations to prior work on hESC cultures.

claim: RPM cell lines (WT or T58A) were associated with a twofold increase in the neuroendocrine compartment when compared with RP cells.
source: These results indicated that RPM cell lines (WT or T58A) were associated with a twofold increase in the neuroendocrine compartment when compared with RP cells (p<2.2 × 10–16; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Statistical finding from differential cluster abundance analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: RPM tumors had a threefold enrichment of cells expressing neuroendocrine markers compared to RP cell lines.
source: Similarly, RPM tumors had a threefold enrichment of cells expressing neuroendocrine markers compared to RP cell lines (p<2.2 × 10–16).
evidence: Statistical finding from differential cluster abundance analysis.

claim: RPM tumors and cells expressed MYC, not MYCN or MYCL at high levels.
source: Notably, we found that RPM tumors and cells expressed MYC, not MYCN or MYCL at high levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EGFP expression was strongly correlated with MYC (Pearson r=0.45, p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: Moreover, EGFP expression was strongly correlated with MYC (Pearson r=0.45, p<2.2 × 10–16) and not MYCN (Pearson r=0.00043, p=0.97) nor MYCL (Pearson r=–0.031, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: EGFP expression was not correlated with MYCN (Pearson r=0.00043, p=0.97).
source: Moreover, EGFP expression was strongly correlated with MYC (Pearson r=0.45, p<2.2 × 10–16) and not MYCN (Pearson r=0.00043, p=0.97) nor MYCL (Pearson r=–0.031, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: EGFP expression was not correlated with MYCL (Pearson r=–0.031, p=0.002).
source: Moreover, EGFP expression was strongly correlated with MYC (Pearson r=0.45, p<2.2 × 10–16) and not MYCN (Pearson r=0.00043, p=0.97) nor MYCL (Pearson r=–0.031, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: The overexpression of either WT or T58A MYC yielded a larger neuroendocrine compartment.
source: Together, these results suggest that the overexpression of either WT or T58A MYC yielded a larger neuroendocrine compartment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the cluster abundance and correlation analyses.

claim: ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high compartments can be clearly identified by sub-clustering the neuroendocrine differentiation group.
source: By sub-clustering the neuroendocrine differentiation group, we could clearly identify ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high compartments, as well as several other groups of cycling cells that did not cleanly fit into any lung lineage cell identity (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Finding from sub-clustering analysis, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The NE-variant cluster was associated with increased expression of genes highly expressed in variant SCLC (NEUROD1, SCG3, IGFBPL1, SSTR2, and MYC).
source: We conducted differential gene expression to further characterize the NEUROD1-high (abbreviated 'NE-variant') and ASCL1-high (abbreviated 'NE') clusters observed with RPM cells (from cell lines and tumors) and found that the NE-variant cluster was associated with increased expression of genes highly expressed in variant SCLC (NEUROD1, SCG3, IGFBPL1, SSTR2, and MYC) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Finding from differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The NE (or 'NE-classic') cluster was linked to heightened expression of genes ranging from histones (HISTH1B, HISTH1D) to redox processes (MT1E, MT2A).
source: In contrast, the NE (or 'NE-classic') cluster was linked to heightened expression of a variety of genes ranging from histones (HISTH1B, HISTH1D) to redox processes (MT1E, MT2A) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Finding from differential gene expression analysis, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis of the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3).
source: Gene set enrichment analysis of these results in the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3) and pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression results.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis of the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
source: Gene set enrichment analysis of these results in the NE-variant cluster revealed increased expression of genes associated with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (p=6.81 × 10–3) and pancreatic beta cell signaling (p=1.01 × 10–3).
evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis of differential expression results.

claim: The NE-variant cluster was linked to lower levels of oxidative phosphorylation (p=1.07 × 10–25).
source: However, this cluster was also linked to lower levels of oxidative phosphorylation (p=1.07 × 10–25), possibly suggesting these subgroups of cells are biologically different (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Finding from gene set enrichment analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RPM and RPM (T58A) cells were associated with higher expression of genes associated with cells in dividing phases of the cell cycle than were observed in RP cultures.
source: Further examination of the ASCL1-high and NEUROD1-high clusters revealed that, across both clusters, RPM and RPM (T58A) cells were associated with higher expression of genes associated with cells in dividing phases of the cell cycle than were observed in RP cultures.
evidence: Finding from cell cycle analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: RPM cells were associated with a 10-fold increase in G2M cells in the NE cluster compared to RP cultures (p=9.6 × 10–6).
source: We compared the proportion of G2M cells between culture-derived RPM and RP models. This revealed that RPM cells were associated with a 10- and 11-fold increase in the NE and NE-variant clusters, respectively (NE p=9.6 × 10–6, NE-variant p=1.9 × 10–7) with a relative reduction in cells in the G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Statistical finding from cell cycle analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: RPM cells were associated with an 11-fold increase in G2M cells in the NE-variant cluster compared to RP cultures (p=1.9 × 10–7).
source: We compared the proportion of G2M cells between culture-derived RPM and RP models. This revealed that RPM cells were associated with a 10- and 11-fold increase in the NE and NE-variant clusters, respectively (NE p=9.6 × 10–6, NE-variant p=1.9 × 10–7) with a relative reduction in cells in the G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Statistical finding from cell cycle analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The joint density was highest for cells that co-express MYC and NEUROD1 and was localized to the NEUROD1-high cluster.
source: We computed the cellular density of co-expression patterns of cells that express MYC in addition to either ASCL1 or NEUROD1. This identified that the joint density was highest for cells that co-express MYC and NEUROD1 and was localized to the NEUROD1-high cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Finding from co-expression analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ASCL1 and MYC expressions are negatively correlated (Pearson r=–0.11, p=1.5 × 10–4).
source: Similar to what was previously reported by other groups, we found that ASCL1 and MYC expressions are negatively correlated (Pearson r=–0.11, p=1.5 × 10–4).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data, consistent with prior reports.

claim: A modest correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in single-cell data (Pearson r=0.17, p=3.7 × 10–4).
source: Moreover, a modest correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in our single-cell data (Pearson r=0.17, p=3.7 × 10–4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: An extremely strong correlation between MYC and NEUROD1 expression was identified in bulk primary and metastatic RPM tumors (Pearson r=0.93, p=0.02).
source: Although we couldn't determine co-expression within the same cell using bulk gene expression data, we identified an extremely strong correlation between the expression of these two genes (Pearson r=0.93, p=0.02, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis from bulk RNA-seq data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The overexpression of MYC (WT or T58A) may be linked to an SCLC-N phenotype.
source: Taken together, we show that the overexpression of MYC (WT or T58A) may be linked to an SCLC-N phenotype.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the co-expression and correlation analyses.

claim: Enrichment patterns in RPM and RPM (T58A) xenografts revealed that both ASCL1- and NEUROD1-high clusters expressed SCLC-N-associated genes more frequently than SCLC-A and SCLC-P-associated counterparts (p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: Enrichment patterns in RPM and RPM (T58A) xenografts revealed that both ASCL1- and NEUROD1-high clusters expressed SCLC-N-associated genes more frequently than SCLC-A and SCLC-P-associated counterparts (p<2.2 × 10–16, Figure 4G).
evidence: Statistical finding from subtype enrichment score analysis, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: RP cell cultures more closely resembled cells from tumors with an SCLC-A phenotype (p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: In contrast, RP cell cultures more closely resembled cells from tumors with an SCLC-A phenotype (p<2.2 × 10–16, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Statistical finding from subtype enrichment score analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: All RPM xenografts strongly exhibited an SCLC-N transcriptional program.
source: Moreover, we found that all RPM xenografts strongly exhibited an SCLC-N transcriptional program.
evidence: Finding from cellular deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-seq data.

claim: Overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells, encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation, and may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling and subtype analyses, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Overexpression of WT or mutant MYC may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that overexpression of WT or mutant MYC alters the transcriptional identity of RP cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), encouraging neuroendocrine differentiation, and may assist with the transformation from a SCLC-A to SCLC-N phenotype.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling and subtype analyses, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The addition of an efficiently expressed transgene encoding normal or mutant human MYC can convert weakly tumorigenic human PNEC cells into highly malignant, metastatic SCLC-like cancers after implantation into the renal capsule of immunodeficient mice.
source: In this report, we show that the addition of an efficiently expressed transgene encoding normal or mutant human MYC can convert weakly tumorigenic human PNEC cells, derived from a human ESC line and depleted of tumor suppressors RB1 and TP53, into highly malignant, metastatic SCLC-like cancers after implantation into the renal capsule of immunodeficient mice.
evidence: Summary of the main finding of the study, supported by all experimental data presented.

claim: SCLC is a highly aggressive cancer with a relatively stereotypic genotype that is generally recalcitrant to therapeutic strategies that have not changed appreciably in the past 30 years.
source: Because SCLC is a highly aggressive cancer with a relatively stereotypic genotype that is generally recalcitrant to therapeutic strategies that have not changed appreciably in the past 30 years, we have been attempting to generate a model for SCLC in which the cancer cells are human in origin, derived from the most commonly affected pulmonary cell lineage (neuroendocrine), and equipped with the major and most common genotypic and phenotypic changes characteristic of SCLC.
evidence: Established knowledge about SCLC characteristics and treatment history.

claim: The choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC.
source: Our choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on both the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC and the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017; Huijbers et al., 2014; Ciampricotti et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Rationale for experimental design based on known characteristics of human SCLC and prior mouse models.

claim: The choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC.
source: Our choice of MYC to serve as an oncogenic driver in hESC-derived PNECs was based on both the frequent finding of high levels of MYC RNA in human SCLC and the use of Myc overexpression strategies to generate aggressive mouse models of SCLC (Ireland et al., 2020; Mollaoglu et al., 2017; Huijbers et al., 2014; Ciampricotti et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Rationale for experimental design based on prior mouse models, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA.
source: However, not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA, and other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
evidence: Acknowledgment of heterogeneity in human SCLC, based on established knowledge.

claim: Other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
source: However, not all human SCLC tumors have abundant MYC RNA, and other genes, including other members of the MYC gene family, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of SCLC.
evidence: Established knowledge about genetic drivers of SCLC.

claim: The hESC-derived tumors arising from RPM RUES2 cells belong to the SCLC-N subtype.
source: Transcriptional profiling has also allowed us to conclude that the hESC-derived tumors arising from RPM RUES2 cells belong to the SCLC-N subtype, one of the major subtypes of SCLC now recognized by several laboratories and clinicians studying SCLC.
evidence: Conclusion from transcriptional profiling analysis presented in the study.

claim: It is unclear whether SCLC-N truly represents a subtype of SCLC with distinct outcomes and therapeutic sensitivities, or rather a snapshot from a continuum in tumor evolution driven (principally) by MYC toward an aggressive, recalcitrant disease.
source: It is unclear whether SCLC-N truly represents a subtype of SCLC with distinct outcomes and therapeutic sensitivities (Gay et al., 2021), or rather a snapshot from a continuum in tumor evolution driven (principally) by MYC toward an aggressive, recalcitrant disease (Choudhuri et al., 2023; Pongor et al., 2023).
evidence: Discussion of uncertainty in the field, supported by citations to conflicting perspectives.

claim: Metastatic spread was observed from RPM tumors growing initially in the renal capsule but not from primary subcutaneous tumors initiated with the same cell culture.
source: Finally, we note that in the experiments reported here, metastatic spread was observed from RPM tumors growing initially in the renal capsule but not from primary subcutaneous tumors initiated with the same cell culture.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations comparing injection sites.

claim: Metastatic spread may depend on the site(s) of growth of the primary tumor.
source: It may prove important to test other sites of primary tumor growth with RPM cells from the RUES2 line or with other SCLC models, to determine the degree to which metastatic spread depends on the site(s) of growth of the primary tumor and to identify specific factors that promote such spread.
evidence: Speculation about future experiments based on current observations.
